claim: TRPC3 and NALCN channels together form sustained inward currents responsible for the slow depolarization of nigral DA neurons.
source: Here we show that TRPC3 and NALCN channels together form sustained inward currents responsible for the slow depolarization of nigral DA neurons.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract, supported by multiple experimental approaches including pharmacological blockade, knockout mice studies, and electrophysiological recordings throughout the manuscript.

claim: Specific TRPC3 channel blockade completely blocked DA neuron pacemaking in wild-type mice.
source: Specific TRPC3 channel blockade completely blocked DA neuron pacemaking
evidence: Demonstrated by application of pyr10 and pyr3 (specific TRPC3 blockers) which eliminated spontaneous firing in WT mice, shown in Figures 1E, 1F, and 3B.

claim: Pacemaking activity in TRPC3 knockout mice was perfectly normal.
source: but the pacemaking activity in TRPC3 knock-out (KO) mice was perfectly normal, suggesting the presence of compensating ion channels.
evidence: Shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, where spontaneous firing rate and electrical properties did not differ between TRPC3 KO and WT mice.

claim: Blocking NALCN channels abolished pacemaking in both TRPC3 KO and wild-type mice.
source: Blocking NALCN channels abolished pacemaking in both TRPC3 KO and wild-type mice.
evidence: Demonstrated by application of L-703,606 (NALCN blocker) which stopped spontaneous firing in both WT and TRPC3 KO mice, shown in Figures 4A and 4E-G.

claim: NALCN current is increased in TRPC3 KO mice.
source: The NALCN current and mRNA and protein expression are increased in TRPC3 KO mice, indicating that NALCN compensates for TRPC3 currents.
evidence: Shown by neurotensin-evoked NALCN currents being significantly larger in TRPC3 KO mice (Figure 5A-B), qRT-PCR showing increased NALCN mRNA (Figure 5C-D), and western blot showing increased NALCN protein (Figure 5E-F).

claim: NALCN mRNA expression is increased in TRPC3 KO mice.
source: The NALCN current and mRNA and protein expression are increased in TRPC3 KO mice, indicating that NALCN compensates for TRPC3 currents.
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR showing significantly higher NALCN mRNA levels in both SNc tissues and single DA neurons from TRPC3 KO mice compared to WT (Figure 5C-D).

claim: NALCN protein expression is increased in TRPC3 KO mice.
source: The NALCN current and mRNA and protein expression are increased in TRPC3 KO mice, indicating that NALCN compensates for TRPC3 currents.
evidence: Shown by western blot analysis demonstrating significantly increased NALCN protein in heterozygous and homozygous TRPC3 KO mice compared to WT littermates (Figure 5E-F).

claim: TRPC3 and NALCN contribute equally to slow depolarization in normal conditions.
source: In normal conditions, TRPC3 and NALCN contribute equally to slow depolarization.
evidence: Demonstrated by membrane potential measurements showing that pyr10 and L-703,606 hyperpolarized the membrane potential to the same extent in WT mice (Figure 6), and relative contribution analysis showing approximately equal contributions (Figure 6D).

claim: Midbrain dopamine neurons are slow pacemakers that maintain extracellular DA levels.
source: Midbrain dopamine (DA) neurons are slow pacemakers that maintain extracellular DA levels.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by citations to Grace and Bunney, 1984 and others in the introduction.

claim: Subthreshold slow depolarization underlies autonomous pacemaking and determines its rate during interspike intervals.
source: During the interspike intervals, subthreshold slow depolarization underlies autonomous pacemaking and determines its rate.
evidence: Demonstrated by correlation between slope of slow depolarization and firing frequency (Figure 1D), and by the ability to restore pacemaking with leak-like current injection (Figures 2 and 4).

claim: Most SNc DA neurons recorded from midbrain slices exhibited a very regular firing rhythm with an average firing rate of 3.28 ± 0.13 Hz.
source: Most SNc DA neurons recorded from midbrain slices exhibited a very regular firing rhythm with an average firing rate of 3.28 ± 0.13 Hz (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, n = 17).
evidence: Direct measurement from electrophysiological recordings reported in the results section.

claim: Phase II of slow depolarization occupies more than 3/4 of the interspike interval.
source: Phase II, occupying more than 3/4 of the interspike interval (Figure 1C), most clearly denotes slow depolarization (Figure 1B, green dotted line).
evidence: Shown in pie chart in Figure 1C indicating Phase II comprises 77% of the interspike interval duration.

claim: Isradipine and ZD-7288 do not affect spontaneous firing rate of SNc DA neurons.
source: As previously reported (Kim et al., 2007; Guzman et al., 2009), they do not affect spontaneous firing rate at all (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B), indicating that L-type Ca2+ and HCN channels are not essential for pacemaking.
evidence: Demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings showing no significant change in firing rate after application of isradipine (L-type Ca2+ channel blocker) or ZD-7288 (HCN channel blocker), shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: L-type Ca2+ and HCN channels are not essential for pacemaking of SNc DA neurons.
source: indicating that L-type Ca2+ and HCN channels are not essential for pacemaking.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of effect of isradipine and ZD-7288 on spontaneous firing rate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), confirmed in both brain slices and acutely dissociated neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: SKF-96365 and 2-APB strongly inhibited the spontaneous firing of DA neurons in midbrain slices.
source: Consistent with this report, nonspecific TRPC channel blockers, such as SKF-96365 and 2-ABP, strongly inhibited the spontaneous firing of DA neurons in the midbrain slices (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Shown by electrophysiological recordings in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-D demonstrating complete or near-complete cessation of firing upon application of these blockers.

claim: Pyr3 and pyr10 completely abolished spontaneous firing of DA neurons in midbrain slices.
source: These channel blockers completely abolished spontaneous firing of DA neurons in the midbrain slices (Figure 1E,F)
evidence: Demonstrated by whole-cell recordings showing cessation of firing upon application of pyr3 or pyr10 (Figure 1E-F).

claim: 92% of TH-positive DA neurons in SNc overlap with TRPC3-positive neurons.
source: Double immunofluorescence staining of the midbrain slices containing the SNc (Figure 1H,I; Clapham et al., 2005) showed that TH-positive DA neurons were mostly overlapped with TRPC3-positive neurons (overlaps = 92%).
evidence: Shown by double immunofluorescence staining and quantification in Figure 1H-I.

claim: All examined isolated SNc DA neurons expressed TRPC3 mRNA.
source: In addition, single-cell RT-PCR from the isolated SNc DA neurons showed expression of TRPC3 mRNA in all cells examined (Figure 1J).
evidence: Demonstrated by single-cell RT-PCR showing TRPC3 expression in all 10 cells examined (Figure 1J).

claim: Pyr10 eliminated slow depolarization and spontaneous firing completely in SNc DA neurons.
source: In SNc DA neurons of midbrain slices, pyr10 eliminated slow depolarization and spontaneous firing completely (Figures 1E and 2A).
evidence: Shown by voltage traces in Figures 1E and 2A demonstrating complete cessation of firing and loss of slow depolarization upon pyr10 application.

claim: Injection of continuous current revived spontaneous firing after pyr10 blockade, at a rate correlated with injected current size.
source: Under this condition, the injection of a small amount of continuous current, which resembles a leak current, revived spontaneous firing, at a rate that correlated with an injected current size (Figure 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by current-clamp recordings showing dose-dependent restoration of firing with increasing current injection (Figure 2A-B).

claim: Voltage traces of regenerated slow depolarization and action potential after pyr10 treatment with current injection were completely aligned with those before pyr10 treatment.
source: When the firing rate was resuscitated to the control level, voltage traces of the regenerated slow depolarization and action potential were completely aligned with those before pyr10 treatment (Figure 2A, right bottom; Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Shown by overlapping voltage traces in Figure 2A (right bottom) and detailed analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing no significant differences in phase durations, slopes, or AHP.

claim: The channel inhibited by pyr10 is a leak-like channel.
source: indicating that the channel inhibited by pyr10 could be a leak-like channel.
evidence: Inferred from the ability to completely restore normal pacemaking with continuous linear current injection that mimics leak current (Figure 2).

claim: Pyr10 hyperpolarized the membrane potential more strongly than isradipine in the presence of TTX.
source: In contrast, pyr10 not only suppressed SOPs but also hyperpolarized membrane potentials more strongly than isradipine (Figure 2D,E)
evidence: Shown by membrane potential measurements in Figure 2D-E demonstrating greater hyperpolarization with pyr10 compared to isradipine.

claim: Replacement of external Na+ with NMDG further hyperpolarized the membrane potential after pyr10 treatment.
source: After pyr10 hyperpolarized the membrane potential, the total replacement of external Na+ with equimolar large cation N-methyl-d-glucamine (NMDG) further hyperpolarized the membrane potential (Figure 2E)
evidence: Demonstrated by membrane potential measurements showing additional hyperpolarization upon NMDG substitution (Figure 2E).

claim: The spontaneous firing rate of DA neurons in TRPC3 KO mice did not differ from that of wild-type littermates.
source: Surprisingly, the spontaneous firing of DA neurons in TRPC3 KO mice survived, and the spontaneous firing rate did not differ from that of wild-type (WT) littermates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, n = 23, p=0.23).
evidence: Shown by statistical comparison of firing rates between TRPC3 KO and WT mice in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C (p=0.23, n=23).

claim: There were no significant differences in electrical properties of DA neurons between TRPC3 KO and WT mice.
source: Moreover, we could not find any significant difference in many electrical properties of DA neurons between TRPC3 KO and WT mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–I)
evidence: Demonstrated by comparisons of action potential peaks, afterhyperpolarization, spike thresholds, input resistance, and cell capacitance showing no significant differences (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-H, all p>0.05).

claim: Pyr10 did not affect the spontaneous firing rate of DA neurons in TRPC3 KO mice.
source: Interestingly, in the TRPC3 KO mice, the application of pyr10 did not affect the spontaneous firing rate of DA neurons at all (Figure 3B,C)
evidence: Shown by electrophysiological recordings in Figure 3B-C demonstrating no change in firing rate upon pyr10 application in TRPC3 KO mice (p>0.05).

claim: Pyr10 completely blocked the pacemaking of DA neurons in WT mice.
source: whereas pyr10 completely blocked the pacemaking of DA neurons in the WT mice (Figure 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by recordings showing complete cessation of firing in WT mice upon pyr10 application (Figure 3B-C).

claim: The inhibitory action of pyr10 on DA neuron pacemaking in WT mice is mediated by selective TRPC3 channel antagonism.
source: These data strongly indicate that the inhibitory action of pyr10 on DA neuron pacemaking in WT mice should be mediated by selective TRPC3 channel antagonism.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of pyr10 in WT (complete block) versus TRPC3 KO mice (no effect), shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: SKF-96365 did not affect the pacemaking rate of DA neurons in TRPC3 KO mice.
source: In addition, unlike WT mice, SKF-96365, which blocks all members of TRPC channels (Nilius and Flockerzi, 2014; Hahn et al., 2020), did not affect the pacemaking rate of DA neurons in TRPC3 KO mice (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: Shown by electrophysiological recordings in Figure 3B-C demonstrating no change in firing rate upon SKF-96365 application in TRPC3 KO mice (p>0.05).

claim: Pyr10 hyperpolarized the membrane potential of DA neurons in WT mice but not in TRPC3 KO mice.
source: Under this condition, pyr10 hyperpolarized the membrane potential of DA neurons in WT mice as expected (Figure 3D, left), but not in TRPC3 KO mice (Figure 3D, right).
evidence: Demonstrated by membrane potential measurements in acutely dissociated neurons showing significant hyperpolarization in WT but not in TRPC3 KO mice (Figure 3D-F).

claim: L-703,606 completely abolished pacemaking of SNc DA neurons.
source: Therefore, we applied L-703,606 to SNc DA neurons in midbrain slices and observed the complete abolition of pacemaking (Figure 4A).
evidence: Shown by electrophysiological recordings in Figure 4A demonstrating cessation of spontaneous firing upon L-703,606 application.

claim: Step-by-step linear current injections restored regular pacemaking activity after L-703,606 blockade.
source: Under this condition, step-by-step linear current injections by whole-cell patch pipette to the neuron restored regular pacemaking activity (Figure 4B,D)
evidence: Demonstrated by current-clamp recordings showing dose-dependent restoration of firing with increasing current injection (Figure 4B, D).

claim: Voltage traces between revived firings after L-703,606 treatment and those before treatment were completely aligned when firing rate was restored to control level.
source: When the firing rate was resuscitated to the control level, the voltage traces between the revived firings and those before L-703,606 treatment were completely aligned to each other (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Shown by overlapping voltage traces in Figure 4C and detailed analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 showing no significant differences in phase durations, slopes, or AHP.

claim: L-703,606 hyperpolarized the membrane potential to the same extent as TRPC3 blockers in WT mice.
source: After pretreatment with TTX and ZD-7288, the application of L-703,606 hyperpolarized the membrane potential to the same extent as TRPC3 blockers in the acutely dissociated DA neurons of WT mice
evidence: Shown by membrane potential measurements in Figure 4E-G and comparison with pyr10 effects in Figure 6.

claim: L-703,606 resulted in greater hyperpolarization of the membrane potential in TRPC3 KO mice compared to WT mice.
source: but resulted in greater hyperpolarization of the membrane potential in TRPC3 KO mice (Figure 4E–G).
evidence: Demonstrated by membrane potential measurements showing significantly larger hyperpolarization in TRPC3 KO mice compared to WT (Figure 4E-G, p<0.01).

claim: NT-evoked NALCN currents in dissociated DA neurons from TRPC3 KO mice were significantly larger than those in WT mice.
source: The NT-evoked NALCN currents in dissociated DA neurons from TRPC KO mice were significantly larger than those in WT mice (Figure 5A,B)
evidence: Demonstrated by whole-cell voltage-clamp recordings showing larger current amplitudes in TRPC3 KO mice (Figure 5A-B, p=0.0019).

claim: Expression of NALCN mRNAs in TRPC3 KO mice was significantly higher than in WT mice in both SNc tissues and dissociated single DA neurons.
source: In both cases, the expression of NALCN mRNAs in TRPC3 KO mice was significantly higher than in WT mice.
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR from SNc tissues (Figure 5C, p<0.05) and single DA neurons (Figure 5D, p<0.05).

claim: mRNAs of other members of TRPC channels in TRPC3 KO mice were not changed.
source: However, mRNAs of the other members of TRPC channels in TRPC3 KO mice were not changed (Figure 5C).
evidence: Shown by qRT-PCR analysis in Figure 5C demonstrating no significant changes in TRPC1, 2, 4, 5, 6, or 7 mRNA levels.

claim: NALCN proteins were significantly increased in heterozygous and homozygous TRPC3 KO mice compared to WT littermates.
source: Furthermore, using western blot analysis, we confirmed that NALCN proteins were more significantly increased in heterozygous and homozygous TRPC3 KO mice than in WT littermates (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis showing increased NALCN protein expression in TRPC3 heterozygous and KO mice (Figure 5E-F, p<0.05).

claim: ZD-7288 did not affect pyr10- or L-703,606-induced hyperpolarization of membrane potentials in SNc DA neurons.
source: After silencing SNc DA neurons with TTX treatment, the application of pyr10 or L-703,606 hyperpolarized the membrane potential to the same extent, but the extent of hyperpolarization was not affected by ZD-7288 in both cases (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: Shown by membrane potential measurements in Figure 6A-B comparing effects with and without ZD-7288 pretreatment.

claim: Co-application of pyr10 and L-703,606 without ZD-7288 resulted in hyperpolarization similar to single treatment with each blocker.
source: Ironically, when both pyr10 and L-703,606 were co-applied to SNc DA neurons without ZD-7288, the hyperpolarization was similar to those induced by a single treatment with each blocker (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by membrane potential measurements in Figure 6A-B showing no additive effect of combined blockers without ZD-7288.

claim: In the presence of ZD-7288, co-application of pyr10 and L-703,606 further hyperpolarized the membrane potential.
source: However, in the presence of ZD-7288, the co-application of pyr10 and L-703,606 further hyperpolarized the membrane potential (Figure 6)
evidence: Shown by membrane potential measurements in Figure 6A-C demonstrating significant additional hyperpolarization with combined blockers in presence of ZD-7288.

claim: HCN channels activate in response to sufficiently significant hyperpolarization of the membrane potential in SNc DA neurons.
source: Therefore, HCN channels appear to activate in response to sufficiently significant hyperpolarization of the membrane potential in SNc DA neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ZD-7288 only affects membrane potential when both TRPC3 and NALCN are blocked together, causing sufficient hyperpolarization (Figure 6).

claim: TRPC3 and NALCN channels contribute equally to more than two-thirds of the leak conductance responsible for slow depolarization in SNc DA neurons.
source: Analysis of the degrees of hyperpolarization induced by pyr10 and/or L-703,606 in the presence of ZD-7288 (Figure 6D) suggests that the TRPC3 and NALCN channels contribute equally to more than two-thirds of the leak conductance responsible for slow depolarization in SNc DA neurons.
evidence: Shown by quantitative analysis in Figure 6D demonstrating TRPC3 contributes ~36%, NALCN ~37%, with ~27% from other sources.

claim: DA neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta are essential for controlling motivational parts of brain functions such as voluntary movement, action selection, future movement, and reward-based learning.
source: Dopamine (DA) neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) are essential for controlling the motivational parts of brain functions such as voluntary movement, action selection, future movement, and reward-based learning (Grace and Bunney, 1984; Schultz, 2007; da Silva et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Dysfunction of DA neurons is associated with many neuropsychiatric diseases including Parkinson's disease and schizophrenia.
source: Dysfunction of DA neurons is associated with many neuropsychiatric diseases including Parkinson's disease and schizophrenia (Bozzi and Borrelli, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citation.

claim: Midbrain DA neurons continuously generate spontaneous action potentials, sustaining ambient DA levels in target areas including the striatum.
source: Midbrain DA neurons are slow pacemakers that continuously generate spontaneous action potentials, consequentially sustaining ambient DA levels in target areas including the striatum (Grace et al., 2007; Morikawa and Paladini, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: In response to unexpected reward stimuli, DA neurons produce high-frequency burst discharges that accompany DA surges.
source: However, in response to unexpected reward stimuli, DA neurons also produce high-frequency burst discharges that accompany DA surges (Schultz, 1998; Schultz, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: The rate and regularity of DA neuron pacemaking are robust against many kinds of pharmacological and molecular perturbations.
source: The rate and regularity of DA neuron pacemaking are robust against many kinds of pharmacological and molecular perturbations including most known specific blockers for classical candidate pacemaker ion channels, such as HCN and voltage-activated Ca2+ channels (VACCs; Paladini et al., 2003; Kim et al., 2007; Guzman et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations and confirmed by experimental data in this study.

claim: The key feature of DA neuron pacemaking is the subthreshold slow depolarization during interspike intervals that requires a non-voltage-dependent background sodium current.
source: The key feature of DA neuron pacemaking is the subthreshold slow depolarization during interspike intervals that requires a non-voltage-dependent background sodium current (Khaliq and Bean, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Khaliq and Bean, 2010.

claim: Robust pacemaking of SNc DA neurons depends on leak-like nonselective cation channels that constitutively open at relatively hyperpolarized membrane potentials.
source: At present, the dominant view is that, in SNc DA neurons, robust pacemaking depends on leak-like nonselective cation channels that constitutively open at relatively hyperpolarized membrane potentials.
evidence: This represents the current understanding in the field, which the study aims to address by identifying specific channels.

claim: Pacemaking of DA neurons is only stopped by SKF-96365 and 2-APB, nonspecific blockers for nonselective cation channels.
source: So far, the pacemaking of DA neurons is only stopped by SKF-96365 and 2-aminoethoxydiphenyl borate (2-APB), nonspecific blockers for nonselective cation channels (Kim et al., 2007) that are also blockers for transient receptor potential-canonical (TRPC) channels (Nilius and Flockerzi, 2014; Lievremont et al., 2005).
evidence: This is based on previous work (Kim et al., 2007) and confirmed in this study (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-D).

claim: TRPC3 channels have constitutive voltage-independent activities at very low membrane potentials.
source: Among several members of the TRPC family, TRPC3 may be a potential candidate for pacemaker channels in DA neurons because of its constitutive voltage-independent activities at very low membrane potentials (Dietrich et al., 2003; Zhou et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about TRPC3 channel properties, supported by citations.

claim: NALCN has been identified as the background Na+ leak channel that determines resting Na+ permeability and neuronal excitability in the central nervous system.
source: Recently, NALCN has been identified as the background Na+ leak channel that determines resting Na+ permeability and neuronal excitability in the central nervous system (Lu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about NALCN, supported by citation to Lu et al., 2007.

claim: NALCN contributes to resting membrane potentials and endogenous activities in several neurons.
source: There is increasing evidence that NALCN contributes to the resting membrane potentials and endogenous activities in several neurons (Lu et al., 2007; Lu et al., 2009; Shi et al., 2016; Lutas et al., 2016; Yeh et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: In SNc DA neurons of conditional NALCN knockout mice, spontaneous firing activity was severely decreased in most cells.
source: In the SNc DA neuron of conditional NALCN knockout (KO) mice, spontaneous firing activity was severely decreased in most cells (Philippart and Khaliq, 2018)
evidence: This is based on previous work by Philippart and Khaliq, 2018.

claim: TRPC3 and NALCN are two major leak channels essential for robust pacemaking in SNc DA neurons.
source: In this study, we use TRPC3 KO mice, specific TRPC3 channel blockers (Kiyonaka et al., 2009; Schleifer et al., 2012), and NALCN channel blockers that we recently identified (Hahn et al., 2020) to report that TRPC3 and NALCN are two major leak channels essential for robust pacemaking in SNc DA neurons.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by comprehensive experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Slow depolarization is absolutely necessary for pacemaking of DA neurons.
source: Slow depolarization is absolutely necessary for pacemaking (Nedergaard et al., 1993; Grace and Onn, 1989; Ping and Shepard, 1996) and determines the pacemaking rate (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and confirmed by correlation data in Figure 1D.

claim: A mild and linear slope in the slow depolarization implies the presence of small but continuous depolarizing currents during interspike intervals.
source: A mild and linear slope in the slow depolarization (Figure 1B) implies the presence of small but continuous depolarizing currents during interspike intervals.
evidence: This is inferred from the characteristics of the slow depolarization phase shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Isradipine weakly reduced the afterhyperpolarization possibly via reduced SK channel currents by decreasing Ca2+ influx.
source: Nevertheless, during interspike intervals, isradipine weakly reduced the afterhyperpolarization possibly via reduced SK channel currents by decreasing Ca2+ influx (Poetschke et al., 2015)
evidence: This is observed in the data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,G) and explained based on known mechanisms cited from Poetschke et al., 2015.

claim: ZD-7288 increased slightly afterhyperpolarization, but the increase was too small to affect the firing rate.
source: On the other hand, ZD-7288 increased slightly afterhyperpolarization (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F,G), but the increase was too small to affect the firing rate.
evidence: Shown by measurements in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F-G demonstrating small but significant increase in afterhyperpolarization without effect on firing rate.

claim: Results from midbrain slices are not related to incomplete channel antagonism in brain slice experiments or perturbation of intracellular milieu by whole-cell pipette solution.
source: Regarding the pharmacological effects on firing inhibition, we obtained the same results from the cell-attached patch-clamp recordings in the freshly dissociated single SNc DA neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), indicating that our results from the midbrain slices are not related to either incomplete channel antagonism in brain slice experiments (Guzman et al., 2009) or perturbation of the intracellular milieu by whole-cell pipette solution (Zolles et al., 2006).
evidence: Demonstrated by replicating key findings in acutely dissociated neurons using cell-attached recordings (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: Pyr10-inhibited channels are able to depolarize the membrane potential even in the more hyperpolarized state.
source: In contrast, pyr10 not only suppressed SOPs but also hyperpolarized membrane potentials more strongly than isradipine (Figure 2D,E), indicating that pyr10-inhibited channels are able to depolarize the membrane potential even in the more hyperpolarized state.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that pyr10 causes greater hyperpolarization than isradipine (Figure 2D-E), suggesting the blocked channels are active at more hyperpolarized potentials.

claim: TRPC3 substantially contributes to slow depolarization of the membrane potential in DA neurons, but not alone.
source: All these data suggest that TRPC3 substantially contributes to slow depolarization of the membrane potential in DA neurons, but not alone.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that NMDG replacement causes additional hyperpolarization beyond pyr10 effect (Figure 2E), indicating other Na+-permeable channels are present.

claim: The leak-like inward current induced by TRPC3 channels appears to be completely compensated by SKF-96365-resistant and Na+-permeable ion channels in TRPC3 KO mice.
source: Therefore, it is highly likely that the leak-like inward current induced by TRPC3 channels appears to be completely compensated by SKF-96365-resistant and Na+-permeable ion channels in TRPC3 KO mice.
evidence: Inferred from the observations that: (1) pacemaking is normal in TRPC3 KO mice, (2) SKF-96365 has no effect in TRPC3 KO mice, and (3) NMDG replacement still hyperpolarizes membrane potential in TRPC3 KO mice.

claim: NALCN compensates for TRPC3 currents in TRPC3 KO mice.
source: The NALCN current and mRNA and protein expression are increased in TRPC3 KO mice, indicating that NALCN compensates for TRPC3 currents.
evidence: Supported by increased NALCN currents (Figure 5A-B), mRNA (Figure 5C-D), and protein (Figure 5E-F) in TRPC3 KO mice, along with functional data showing L-703,606 blocks pacemaking in TRPC3 KO mice.

claim: NALCN channels compensate the TRPC3-mediated sustained depolarizing current essential for pacemaking in SNc DA neurons in TRPC3 KO mice.
source: All these data indicate that NALCN could be another nonselective cation channel essential for the pacemaking of SNc DA neurons. In TRPC3 KO mice, NALCN channels appear to compensate the TRPC3-mediated sustained depolarizing current essential for pacemaking in SNc DA neurons.
evidence: Supported by the combination of: (1) L-703,606 blocking pacemaking in both WT and TRPC3 KO mice, (2) increased NALCN expression in TRPC3 KO mice, and (3) greater L-703,606-induced hyperpolarization in TRPC3 KO mice.

claim: This is the first report to uncover molecular identities and properties of leak channels responsible for the pacemaking in SNc DA neurons.
source: This is the first report to uncover molecular identities and properties of leak channels responsible for the pacemaking in SNc DA neurons.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings, based on the comprehensive identification of TRPC3 and NALCN as the major leak channels.

claim: Slow depolarization driven by multiple leak channels provides the reason why DA neuron pacemaking is robust and resistant to many kinds of pharmacological and molecular perturbations.
source: This slow depolarization driven by multiple leak channels provides the reason why DA neuron pacemaking is robust and resistant to many kinds of pharmacological and molecular perturbations (Guzman et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that two major leak channels (TRPC3 and NALCN) can compensate for each other, explaining the robustness of pacemaking.

claim: TRPC3 and NALCN channels primarily conduct Na+ ions under physiological conditions.
source: Although TRPC3 and NALCN channels belong to NSCCs, they primarily conduct Na+ ions under physiological conditions (Lu et al., 2007; Cochet-Bissuel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about these channels, supported by citations.

claim: The main characteristic of TRPC3 and NALCN channels is their constitutive activation at very low membrane potentials and the linearity of the IV relationship in the subthreshold range of the membrane potential.
source: The main characteristic of these two channels is their constitutive activation at very low membrane potentials and the linearity of the IV relationship in the subthreshold range of the membrane potential (Dietrich et al., 2003; Zhou et al., 2008; Lu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about these channels, supported by citations.

claim: TRPC3 and NALCN channels are responsible for about 66.7% of the subthreshold leak current.
source: Na+ substitution experiments show that these two channels are responsible for about 66.7% of the subthreshold leak current, but do not cover the entire leak current completely.
evidence: Calculated from the relative contribution analysis shown in Figure 6D (36% + 37% = 73%, with ~27% from others, suggesting ~67% from TRPC3 and NALCN combined).

claim: HCN channels can participate in the depolarization of the membrane potential under over-hyperpolarized conditions when TRPC3 and NALCN channels are blocked completely.
source: Of course, HCN channels can also contribute to depolarization under excessively hyperpolarized conditions. In fact, when these two main channels are blocked completely, HCN channels can participate in the depolarization of the membrane potential in the over-hyperpolarized conditions.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ZD-7288 causes additional hyperpolarization only when both TRPC3 and NALCN are blocked (Figure 6C).

claim: Loss of specific ion channels can often be compensated by other channels due to homeostatic mechanisms in neural intrinsic excitability.
source: In the neural intrinsic excitability, loss of specific ion channels can often be compensated by other channels due to homeostatic mechanisms (Marder and Goaillard, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about neural homeostasis, supported by citation.

claim: Other members of the TRPC family do not appear to compensate the pacemaking in TRPC3 KO mice.
source: Therefore, other members of the TRPC family do not appear to compensate the pacemaking in TRPC3 KO mice.
evidence: Inferred from: (1) SKF-96365 (which blocks all TRPC channels) has no effect in TRPC3 KO mice, and (2) mRNA levels of other TRPC channels are not increased in TRPC3 KO mice (Figure 5C).

claim: NALCN and TRPC3 channels have many binding proteins and upstream regulators, including neurotransmitters and hormones.
source: NALCN and TRPC3 channels have many binding proteins and upstream regulators, including neurotransmitters and hormones (Cochet-Bissuel et al., 2014; Amaral and Pozzo-Miller, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about these channels, supported by citations.

claim: The mechanism of pacemaking regulation can play diverse roles in DA neuron functions.
source: Therefore, the mechanism of pacemaking regulation can play diverse roles in DA neuron functions.
evidence: This is speculated based on the multiple regulatory mechanisms of TRPC3 and NALCN channels.
